analysis.one_liner: Extends copyright owners' exclusive rights to digital transmissions and bans devices that bypass copy protections.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill applying copyright law to the internet received two Judiciary hearings but never reached a vote, dying when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite copyright law for the digital age. It would treat sending a copyrighted work over a network as distributing it, make importing digital copies without permission an infringement, and make it illegal to import, make, or sell any device or service whose main purpose is to get around copy-protection systems. It also adds some accommodations: libraries could make up to three copies including digital ones for preservation, and nonprofits could freely produce Braille, large-type, and audio editions for blind readers when publishers haven't served that market.
analysis.who_benefits: Copyright owners — record labels, film studios, book publishers, and software companies — would gain a legal claim over digital distribution of their works and new tools to block circumvention technology, with statutory damages of $200 to $25,000 per violation and criminal penalties. Libraries and nonprofits serving visually impaired readers would get narrower but real new freedoms to copy and distribute works in accessible formats.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Copyright holders, plus libraries and blind readers

how_it_helps.text: Copyright owners would gain the exclusive right to distribute copies of their works by transmission, closing what sponsors saw as a gap in the law for the networked environment [S2][S3].

The bill would ban making, importing, or distributing devices or services whose primary purpose or effect is to circumvent copy-protection systems, backed by statutory damages of $200 to $2,500 per device and, for fraudulent tampering with copyright management information, fines up to $500,000 and five years in prison [S2][S3].
Libraries and archives could reproduce up to three copies of a work (up from one) and make digital copies for preservation, security, and replacement of damaged or lost works [S2][S3].

Nonprofit organizations could reproduce and distribute Braille, large-type, and audio editions of published works to visually impaired readers at cost, whenever publishers have not entered that market within a year of publication [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary internet users, libraries' patrons, and technology companies would bear the cost. Anyone sending a copyrighted work over a network could be liable for infringement, and the device ban would reach tools and services that can bypass digital copy protection — potentially including tools with substantial legitimate uses. Fair use and library lending would operate inside tighter constraints, since only one of a library's three permitted copies could be distributed and reproduced copies would need a copyright notice.
analysis.who_pays_short: Internet users, libraries, and device makers

drawbacks.text: The anti-circumvention ban reaches any device or service whose 'primary purpose or effect' is to bypass a protection system, with no exception for tools that have significant legitimate uses — a rule that could outlaw technology consumers own and use lawfully, and that would effectively let copyright owners control access beyond what copyright law itself grants [S3].

Statutory damages of $200 to $2,500 per device or service, treble damages for repeat violations, and criminal penalties would fall on individuals and small distributors as well as commercial pirates [S3].

The library provisions tighten as much as they loosen: although libraries could hold three copies, only one could be distributed, reproduction would require a copyright notice on the copy, and the new rights allow digital copies only for narrow preservation and replacement purposes [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The library and visually impaired provisions are genuine, if modest, public accommodations. But the bill's center of gravity is expanding copyright owners' control over digital networks, and the anti-circumvention ban in particular has no fair-use safeguard — meaning a legal use of a work could still be unlawful to unlock. As drafted, the costs to ordinary users and technology makers outweigh the targeted benefits, and the similar ban that later became law in 1998 has been criticized on exactly these grounds.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, got two hearings including one joint with a House subcommittee, and never came to a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Orrin Hatch introduced the bill on September 28, 1995, together with Senator Patrick Leahy, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Judiciary [S1][S5].
On November 15, 1995, the Judiciary Committee held hearings jointly with the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts and Intellectual Property [S5].
The committee held a second round of hearings on May 7, 1996 [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill was never reported out of committee or voted on, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For this Congress, ordinary internet users and technology makers came out ahead in the narrow sense that the new digital restrictions never took effect. But the framework was not dead: its core provisions — the transmission right and the anti-circumvention ban — reappeared in the next Congress and became law in the Digital Millennium Copyright Act of 1998, while the exemptions for libraries and visually impaired readers survived in weakened form. In the long run, copyright industries gained the durable legal architecture they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Copyright industries, eventually, via the 1998 DMCA

for.name: Orrin Hatch
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-UT), chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and chaired the committee that held two hearings on it but never brought it to a vote.

for.name: Patrick Leahy
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-VT), senior Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Joined Hatch in introducing the bill as its cosponsor.

for.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings on November 15, 1995 (jointly with a House subcommittee) and May 7, 1996, then took no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Republican chairman and the panel's senior Democrat introduced it together — and no opposition appears anywhere in the record; it simply stalled after two hearings.

industries.industry: Copyright industries (record labels, film studios, book publishers, software)
industries.note: The bill gives copyright owners a new exclusive right over digital distribution, bans circumvention technology, and attaches statutory damages and criminal penalties — expanding their control over how ordinary people access and share digital works. The carve-outs for libraries and blind readers are narrow exceptions to that expansion.

Libraries could make up to three copies including digital ones for preservation and replacement, but only one copy could be distributed, a copyright notice would be required, and digital copying would be limited to preservation and replacement purposes.

industries.industry: Nonprofit organizations serving visually impaired readers
industries.note: The bill creates a clear exemption letting nonprofits produce Braille, large-type, and audio editions at cost when publishers have not served that market within a year — a direct benefit to blind readers.

industries.industry: Consumer electronics and internet service companies
industries.note: The ban on importing, manufacturing, or distributing any device or service whose primary purpose or effect is to circumvent copy protection would expose device makers and service providers to damages for building or offering tools that can bypass protection systems, and their customers would lose access to those tools too.
